Doughty means brave, strong, and determined — especially in a way that doesn't quit. A doughty person faces difficulty head-on, keeps going even when things get hard, and does not back down from a fight or a challenge.
Going Deeper — What It Really Means

Think of the bravest, toughest person you can imagine. Not someone who is just fearless for one quick moment, but someone who is stubbornly, persistently courageous — someone who keeps pushing through danger, hardship, or opposition with grit and strength. That is a doughty person.

The word carries three qualities bundled together:

  • Courage — they are not afraid, or they act despite fear
  • Strength — they have real power, whether physical, mental, or moral
  • Tenacity — they don't give up; they endure

This is what sets doughty apart from simply saying "brave." A brave person might do one courageous act. A doughty person is consistently, reliably, stubbornly tough. It describes a quality of character, not just a single deed.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Calling someone doughty is always a compliment — it carries a tone of deep admiration and respect. It sounds noble, even heroic. When a writer calls someone doughty, the reader is meant to admire them.

It is also a somewhat old-fashioned word. You will not hear it in everyday casual conversation — someone would not say "my doughty friend helped me move my sofa." It belongs to literature, history, formal writing, and elevated speech. When it appears in modern writing, it often gives a slightly classical, dignified, or even poetic flavour to the description. It can also occasionally be used with mild humour or irony, calling something small or ordinary "doughty" to give it a comically heroic spin.

The adjective most commonly describes:

  • People — warriors, explorers, campaigners, leaders, athletes, debaters — anyone who fights hard and holds firm
  • Actions or efforts — a doughty resistance, a doughty performance, a doughty campaign
  • Characters in a story — it is very common in literature and historical writing

Examples:

  • "The doughty soldier fought on for hours, refusing to surrender."
  • "She was a doughty campaigner for justice who faced every setback with renewed energy."
  • "The small nation put up a doughty resistance against the invading army."
  • "Despite being the underdog, the doughty boxer refused to go down."
  • "He proved a doughty opponent in the debate, countering every argument sharply."

Notice that in each case, the person or effort is not just doing something brave — they are persisting against real difficulty. That persistence is the heartbeat of the word.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding what makes doughty unique becomes clearer when you place it next to its neighbours:

  • Brave — the broad, general word for having courage. Doughty is more specific: it adds toughness and persistence.
  • Valiant — brave and noble, often used in grand or heroic contexts. Valiant leans more toward nobility and honour; doughty leans more toward raw toughness and refusal to quit.
  • Bold — willing to take risks, confident. Bold is about stepping forward; doughty is about not stepping back.
  • Intrepid — fearless, especially in the face of danger or the unknown. Intrepid has more of an adventurous spirit; doughty is more about grinding endurance.
  • Stalwart — strongly loyal, reliable, and solid. Stalwart emphasises dependability; doughty emphasises fighting spirit.
  • Resolute — firmly determined. Resolute is about mental firmness; doughty adds a sense of physical or combative strength to that firmness.

So if you had to place doughty on a spectrum, it sits at the intersection of courage + strength + stubborn endurance. None of its synonyms alone captures all three at once quite the same way.

The antonyms of doughty are words like:

  • Cowardly — giving in to fear
  • Timid — shrinking from challenge
  • Faint-hearted — lacking the spirit to persist
  • Weak — without strength of character or body
  • Spineless — having no backbone when pressure is applied

Because doughty is formal and old-fashioned, use it when you want to describe someone's toughness in writing, a speech, or an elevated discussion — not in casual texting or small talk. It fits naturally when:

  • You are writing about historical figures or events
  • You want to give someone a dignified, admiring compliment
  • You are writing fiction, especially with a classical or formal tone
  • You want to describe a long, hard struggle or resistance

Quick test — before using the word, ask yourself: Is this person being tough, brave, AND persistent over time? If yes, doughty fits perfectly.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By
Doughty = stubbornly brave and tough — the kind of strength that refuses to give up.
